translations.source_sense_description: fallen, hineinfallen (mit Betonung auf Gewicht, Trägheit und Masse)

glosses: To fall heavily due to lack of energy.

examples.text: He flopped down in front of the television, exhausted from work.

There was [in the clock in Lyons Cathedral] a centre puppet of the Virgin Mary; and close to her, a small pigeon-hole, out of which another and a very ill-looking puppet made one of the most sudden plunges I ever saw accomplished: instantly flopping back again at sight of her, and banging his little door violently, after him.

glosses: To cause to drop heavily.

examples.text: The tired mule flopped its ears forward and trudged on.

glosses: To fail completely; not to be successful at all (of a movie, play, book, song etc.).

examples.text: The latest album flopped and so the studio canceled her contract.

glosses: To pretend to be fouled in sports, such as basketball, hockey (the same as to dive in soccer)

examples.text: It starts with Chris Paul, because Blake didn't really used to flop like that, you know, last year.
While Stern chastised Vogel for on Thursday calling the Heat "the biggest flopping team in the NBA," he did intimate that he sees merit in the sentiment.

glosses: To strike about with something broad and flat, as a fish with its tail, or a bird with its wings; to rise and fall; to flap.

examples.text: The brim of a hat flops.

glosses: To have (a hand) using the community cards dealt on the flop.

examples.text: Both players flopped sets! Cards dealt on the flop: Q95. Player A's hole cards: 55 (making three of a kind: 555). Player B's hole cards: QQ (making three of a kind: QQQ).

glosses: To stay, sleep or live in a place.

examples.text: […] not just the old material goal of "three hots and a place to flop," […]
They have opened up crypts and basements as immense pads where vagrant and impoverished hippies can flop for the night.

glosses: To flip; to reverse (an image).

examples.text: […] in order to flop the image left-to-right, or all printing will appear reversed.
The possibilities of this type of shot are almost limitless. By quartering the screen and duplicating and flopping the picture, a kaleidoscopic effect is achieved.

glosses: To deny someone parole.

examples.text: I've been incarcerated going on 9½ years. I have never been back on the streets or given a chance to prove myself to society. Every time I would meet the parole board they would flop me telling me I would be a threat to society.

glosses: A heavy, passive fall; a plopping down.
A complete failure, especially in the entertainment industry.

examples.text: Well I know your little baby sister / She thinks that I'm a flop / But I guess that you know that it's true / I spent more time at the bottom than the top

glosses: The first three cards turned face-up by the dealer in a community card poker game.

examples.text: The flop didn't help you but probably did help the other hands.
Here are six tips to help you play successfully on the flop (the first three communal cards).
The strength of your hand now has nothing to do with how strong it may have been before the flop.

glosses: A ponded package of dung, as in a cow-flop.

examples.text: "Maybe as you think," he said, "because as I've the misfortune of an accidental slip on a cow-flop therefore I has the inability of an unborn babe, ...
... cowpat or cow-flop, Cow dung, often used dry as heating fuel.
"Cow flop in a neat package is still cow flop. What did Cable stand to gain from the flood?"

Wherever legitimate tracks are found there's always some fresh scat, y'know, poo, flop, dumplings.

glosses: A flophouse.

examples.text: He was kind of worn but the tooth said he'd never lost a fight or slept in a flop.

glosses: Indicating the sound of something flopping.

examples.text: "One step. Steady. Another step. Flop! I got him!"

glosses: Right, squarely, flat-out.

examples.text: She fell flop on the floor.

glosses: With a flopping sound.
Abbreviation of floating-point operation.

examples.text: The Correlator can perform 750 billion ‘flops’, or simple calculations, per second.

glosses: One floating-point operation per second, a unit of measure of processor speed.

examples.text: The gigaflop supercomputers of today are almost useless. What is needed is a teraflop machine. That’s a machine that can run at a trillion flops, a trillion floating-point operations per second, or roughly a thousand times as fast as Cray Y-MP8.

glosses: Having a full and rounded shape; chubby, somewhat overweight.

examples.text: a plump baby; plump cheeks
The god of wine did his plump clusters bring.
My ideal is to be idle and to love a plump girl.

He was a plump little man and we had been walking uphill at a pace—set by him—far too rapid for his short legs. He breathed stertorously, and half the drops which glimmered on his rotund face were not rain but sweat.

glosses: Fat.
Sudden and without reservation; blunt; direct; downright.

examples.text: After the plump statement that the author was at Erceldoune and spake with Thomas.
I've said so haven't I? Plump and plain.

glosses: To grow plump; to swell out.

examples.text: Her cheeks have plumped.

glosses: To make plump; to fill (out) or support; often with up.

examples.text: to plump oysters or scallops by placing them in fresh or brackish water
to plump up the hollowness of their history with improbable miracles

Although Miss Pross, through her long association with a French family, might have known as much of their language as of her own, if she had had a mind, she had no mind in that direction […] So her manner of marketing was to plump a noun-substantive at the head of a shopkeeper without any introduction in the nature of an article […]

glosses: To give a plumper (kind of vote).
To give (a vote), as a plumper.
To favor or decide in favor of.

examples.text: A recent poll by the New York Times found that although most Brazilians plump for arch-rival Argentina as the team they most want to lose, the second-biggest group want Brazil itself to stumble.

glosses: To cast or let drop (something) all at once, suddenly and heavily.

examples.text: to plump a stone into water

glosses: To drop or fall suddenly or heavily, all at once.

examples.text:
September 24, 1712, The Spectator No. 492, letter from a prude
Dulcissa plumps into a chair.

glosses: Directly; suddenly; perpendicularly.

examples.text: I suppose then, that going plump on a flying whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman’s discretion?

glosses: The sound of a sudden heavy fall.

examples.text: As she beheld her, poor Mrs. Mack's heart fluttered up to her mouth, and then dropped with a dreadful plump, into the pit of her stomach.

glosses: A knot or cluster; a group; a crowd.

examples.text: a plump of trees, fowls, or spears
To visit islands and the plumps of men.

glosses: A group of geese flying close together.
